strengths: The paper identifies a useful and underexplored problem: global-scale geolocation from natural audio. Formalizing the task, adapting standard geolocation metrics, and assembling the XCDC evaluation set could provide a valuable foundation for future work.

The empirical study is broad. It compares regression, hierarchical classification, retrieval, explicit species-range inference, oracle checklists, multiple audio/location encoders, temporal pooling methods, and candidate-location galleries. Reporting three-run means and standard deviations for the main results is good practice.

The species-oracle experiments provide an informative diagnostic: complete or partially corrupted species checklists can sharply constrain location, while current audio models fail to recover this potential on complex multi-species recordings.

AG-CLIP substantially outperforms the evaluated regression, classification, and off-the-shelf retrieval approaches on the iNatSounds test set at fine scales, reaching 6.4% city and 17.2% regional accuracy.

The manuscript is clear and visually polished. The appendix supplies architecture diagrams, preprocessing settings, optimization hyperparameters, gallery ablations, compute requirements, and additional XCDC results, supporting reproducibility if the promised code and data are released.
The authors appropriately acknowledge geographic sampling bias and privacy risks. The weak XCDC transfer results are reported candidly rather than concealed.
weaknesses: The central evaluation does not establish geographic generalization. The manuscript uses the existing iNatSounds split but does not explain whether train, validation, and test recordings are separated by location, recording site, recordist, or time. Nearby or repeated-site observations could therefore appear across splits. This is especially consequential because the retrieval gallery contains training coordinates and changing from a uniform gallery to the training-distribution gallery raises city accuracy from 1.3% to 6.6%. A spatially blocked evaluation, nearest-train-location statistics, and duplicate/recordist leakage analysis are necessary before interpreting the results as global audio geolocation rather than interpolation over collection hotspots.

The proposed method is only modestly original and its key auxiliary loss has weak empirical support. Relative to the same retrieval system without the checklist loss, it changes regional accuracy only from 17.0% to 17.2%, while the main gain is at the coarse continent threshold, from 68.5% to 71.2%. No uncertainty or matched-run significance is reported for this ablation, and the paper does not isolate how much performance comes from iNatSounds species-classification pretraining versus the proposed checklist objective.

The comparison to GeoCLAP and TaxaBind is not sufficient to support broad superiority: these models are used off the shelf under acknowledged domain and supervision mismatches, whereas AG-CLIP is trained and pretrained directly on iNatSounds. Strong matched baselines—fine-tuned soundscape models, a plain audio-to-GeoCLIP model with identical training, modern audio encoders, and parameter/compute-controlled alternatives—are missing.

External generalization is poor. On XCDC, AG-CLIP obtains only 4.3% regional accuracy and is worse than hierarchical classification at that scale (5.3%). Using an XCDC gallery raises performance, but that gallery consists of the evaluation locations themselves and therefore represents a different, transductive closed-set setting. This result should not be presented alongside open-world geolocation without sharper qualification.

The spatiotemporal aggregation experiment forms groups using ground-truth H3 location cells. For genuinely unlocated recordings, this grouping cannot be constructed without external location or site identity. Consequently, the reported improvement from 17.2% to 30.4% regional accuracy is an oracle-grouping analysis rather than a deployable geolocation method; the required side information and intended use case need to be stated explicitly.

The movie geo-forensics case study makes an unsupported inference. Divergent predictions from two noisy, out-of-domain models do not “confirm” post-production modality inconsistencies, particularly when even the closest audio-image prediction pair is 4,480 km apart and no ground-truth source location for the inserted audio is established. These examples are hypotheses or illustrations, not evidence of successful forensic detection.

The oracle analysis uses SINR outputs evaluated at the true test coordinate and simulates detection errors only by uniformly deleting species, with no false positives. This is acceptable as an idealized upper bound, but “10 species” performance should not be read as attainable audio performance: randomly retained range species may differ greatly from audible species, and realistic detectors have structured false negatives, false positives, and taxonomic confusions. Potential overlap between SINR's occurrence training data and iNaturalist audio observations is also not audited.

XCDC construction is underspecified for reproducibility: the definitions of spring and dawn across hemispheres, how sunrise was determined, annotation quality, deduplication, and licensing are not described. The manuscript also inconsistently reports 576 versus 579 XCDC locations. Exact split-generation scripts, seeds, model checkpoint provenance, and dataset licenses should accompany the promised release.

The ethics discussion is incomplete for an ecological geolocation benchmark. Besides human privacy, releasing models or precise coordinates may facilitate locating sensitive or endangered species. The paper should discuss coordinate obscuration, access controls, consent and licensing for Xeno-Canto/iNaturalist recordings, and the copyright status of extracted movie or YouTube material.

strengths: Significance: The paper identifies an underexplored and potentially useful problem—global geolocation from natural audio—and provides a broad comparison of regression, classification, retrieval, and species-range approaches on iNatSounds.

Presentation: The problem formulation, distance-based metrics, main method, and principal results are generally easy to follow. Reporting multiple geographic thresholds and three-run variability is helpful.

Empirical scope: The study includes useful diagnostic experiments on audio and location encoders, temporal pooling, retrieval galleries, species-rich recordings, and geographic variation in performance.
Limitations and ethics: The manuscript honestly acknowledges geographic bias and privacy risks rather than concealing them.
weaknesses: Soundness: The evaluation does not establish geographically independent generalization. The paper gives no analysis of spatial, temporal, observer, recording-site, or device overlap across iNatSounds splits. This is particularly consequential for geolocation, where nearby train/test recordings and location-specific recording artifacts can substantially inflate performance. A spatially disjoint split and nearest-training-location analysis are needed.

Soundness: The spatiotemporal aggregation experiment forms groups using ground-truth H3 locations. Geographic coordinates are precisely the unknown variable in this task, so this grouping is unavailable in the stated test setting unless an external station/group identifier is assumed. The reported improvement from 17.2% to 30.4% regional accuracy therefore does not support improved geolocation from audio alone.

Soundness: The species 'oracle' checklists are generated by querying SINR at the true test coordinates and then decoding these coordinate-derived vectors back into locations. This mainly measures the invertibility of a pretrained spatial model's location fingerprint, including extensive presence and absence information; it is not a convincing upper bound based on species actually audible in a recording.

Originality: AG-CLIP is largely GeoCLIP-style retrieval with an auxiliary BCE objective using SINR-generated labels. Its incremental benefit is small at the principal fine scales: 17.0% to 17.2% at 200 km and no improvement at 25 km in Table 2. The larger 2.7-point gain occurs only at the very coarse 2,500 km threshold, weakening the case for a substantial methodological contribution.

Evaluation: The strongest main result depends heavily on a train-distribution location gallery. Table A1 shows city accuracy falling from 6.6% with the train gallery to 1.3–2.9% with uniform galleries. Comparisons against regression and classification consequently mix model quality with a favorable output prior. Strong location-only, nearest-training-location, frequency-prior, and matched-gallery baselines are missing.

Evaluation: XCDC contains only 576 selected recordings, its construction and deduplication procedures are insufficiently specified, and possible overlap with iNaturalist-based pretraining or SINR training data is not examined. The learned methods achieve only 2.5–5.3% regional accuracy with the standard gallery, so this experiment mainly exposes poor transfer rather than validating the proposed approach.

Soundness: The movie study claims that divergent audio and image predictions 'confirm' modality inconsistencies. Four cherry-picked, viewer-flagged examples cannot establish this: either geolocation model can simply be wrong, the scenes are strongly out of distribution, and there is no ground truth, calibrated null distribution, control set, or quantitative detection evaluation.

Reproducibility and presentation: Benchmark and codebase fields are blank, several essential dataset/split details are absent, and the appendix contains numerical inconsistencies—for example, Table A1 reports regional accuracies of 15.0/15.8/17.4%, while the accompanying text states 13.4/14.8/16.4%; the train-gallery size is variously 120K and 137K, and XCDC is variously 576 and 579 examples.

Significance: The paper demonstrates that the task is difficult, but its best realistic model reaches only 17.2% within 200 km and 6.4% within 25 km on a potentially non-spatially-independent split, while performance transfers poorly to XCDC. Without a credible deployment-oriented split or stronger validation, it is unclear that others can reliably build on the headline results.

Ethics: The discussion mentions generic privacy risk but omits biodiversity-specific risks such as exposing locations of endangered species, as well as licensing and consent considerations for Xeno-Canto and YouTube-derived material. These issues require explicit data-release safeguards.

strengths: Significance and originality: The paper establishes a timely, underexplored problem—global geolocation from natural audio—and provides a useful empirical foundation spanning regression, classification, retrieval, species-range reasoning, long recordings, and multi-recording aggregation. XCDC is a potentially valuable benchmark for species-rich soundscapes.

Soundness: The main iNatSounds comparison is broad and generally well controlled, with multiple geographic thresholds, median error, three-run variability for the principal results, oracle contextualization, and ablations over audio encoders, location encoders, pooling methods, and retrieval galleries. AG-CLIP obtains the strongest fine-scale audio-only result, including 6.4% city and 17.2% regional accuracy.

The experiments reveal useful negative results rather than presenting only successes: off-the-shelf soundscape models transfer poorly, species-rich XCDC recordings remain difficult, and sophisticated temporal pooling does not clearly outperform averaging. These findings should help guide subsequent work.

Presentation: The motivation, task definition, methods, and principal findings are clearly organized. Figures illustrating distance scales, spatial performance, candidate galleries, and model structure make the unfamiliar problem accessible.

The limitations and societal-impact discussion appropriately acknowledges geographic sampling bias and privacy risks. The reported compute requirements are modest, and the appendix gives useful implementation details such as preprocessing, optimization, architecture sizes, and inference costs.
weaknesses: Soundness: The species-oracle experiment is partly circular. Its checklist is generated by SINR using the true test coordinate and is then mapped back to a location embedding; near-perfect performance can therefore reflect a high-dimensional geographic fingerprint of SINR rather than species that could realistically be observed or detected in audio. Consequently, the conclusion that detecting ten species enables 37% regional accuracy is stronger than this synthetic experiment supports.

The incremental contribution of the proposed checklist objective is small at the most relevant scales. Relative to the otherwise comparable GeoCLIP configuration in Table 2, adding the checklist loss leaves city accuracy unchanged at 6.4% and changes regional accuracy only from 17.0% to 17.2%, with the main gain at continental scale. Uncertainty is not reported for this ablation, so it is unclear whether the fine-scale gain is meaningful.

The benchmark protocol needs stronger analysis of geographic leakage and shortcut learning. The manuscript does not report whether train and test recordings can share locations, nearby sites, recordists, dates, or recording devices. This is particularly important because the train-location gallery raises city accuracy substantially relative to uniform galleries and performance is strongest in densely sampled regions.

The spatiotemporal aggregation experiment groups test examples using their ground-truth H3 cells. This can represent a known-site deployment scenario, but that assumption should be explicit. No size-matched random-group control or per-group evaluation is provided, so the gains cannot yet be attributed specifically to complementary species evidence rather than oracle grouping, repeated-site effects, or weighting by large groups.

The multimodal geo-forensics claims are unsupported by the four selected qualitative examples. Given the models' roughly 1,000 km median errors, disagreement of several thousand kilometers does not by itself confirm a post-production artifact. Ground-truth provenance, a calibrated null distribution, controls, and a larger evaluation set are needed; this section is better framed as a hypothesis-generating illustration.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The test-set size, group counts and size distribution, exact XCDC collection/filtering procedure, and several baseline-training details are missing or underspecified. The appendix contains stale inconsistencies: XCDC is reported as both 576 and 579 recordings, and the prose for Table A1 cites gallery results that differ from the table. The displayed benchmark/code links are also absent.

The ethics discussion is welcome but brief relative to the surveillance potential of audio geolocation. It should more concretely address consent, misuse mitigation, licensing or redistribution of Xeno-Canto and movie/YouTube material, and risks to sensitive wildlife locations. These concerns are material but do not presently constitute an unresolved ethical bar to publication.
